    Paper, gunpowder and Shibusawa

    Walk the whole circuit of capital in one morning, from the banker's garden down to the factory floor and out to the croquette counter.

    Meet the man in your wallet

    Since July 2024 the face on Japan's ¥10,000 note has been Shibusawa Eiichi. He is the closest thing Japan has to the men at the centre of your books. He was born in 1840 into a well-off family that farmed and sold indigo. He saw Paris in 1867 with the shogun's delegation. He served in the new Finance Ministry, then left in 1873 to run the First National Bank, Japan's first modern bank. In 1882 he and several partners founded the Osaka Spinning Company. By the end he had founded or nursed about 500 companies, and he died a viscount in 1931.

    He also had a creed. He called it the Analects and the abacus: morality and business cannot be pulled apart, and the public interest comes before the money. A protagonist who preaches virtue while building a business empire is exactly the kind you write about "for better and worse". This walk lets you stand in his garden and judge him there.

    What you will see with your own eyes

    You ride the JR line north for about a quarter of an hour and step out at Ōji. East of the station, where the Sun Square complex now stands, Shibusawa's paper company began making paper on imported machines in 1875. A stone marks the birthplace of Western paper in Japan. No mill buildings survive, so you read the site from the Otonashi river park below, the stream that powered Ōji's early mills.

    Then you climb the one hill of the day into Asukayama Park. Edo's first public cherry park became Shibusawa's home from 1879 until his death. From the paths of his old garden you see the outsides of two buildings. They are the Bankōro of 1917 and the Seien Bunko of 1925. Both are Important Cultural Properties. Stand there and look down the slope. The owner lived above his mill, and the view still says so.

    At ten the Paper Museum opens in the same park, for ¥400. It traces machine paper-making from its start at Ōji, through the company's own history. The museum itself is a survivor. It opened in 1950 in the mill's electrical room, the only room left unburned after the air raids, and moved up the hill in 1998.

    Next you walk about a kilometre and a half north to Jūjō. Kita Central Park sits on the ground of the Tokyo Arsenal's Jūjō works, opened in 1905. The army's land later passed to the Self-Defense Forces and then to the ward. Its red-brick building of 1919 reopened in 2008 as the ward's Central Library. You can walk in for free and see how the old works hall was kept.

    Lunch is on Jūjō Ginza, one of Tokyo's cheapest shopping streets, with about 200 low-rise shops. A pork menchi cost ¥129 there in 2020. You eat standing, among the shoppers, for well under a thousand yen. Then a short walk to Higashi-Jūjō and the train home.

    Why paper, and why an arsenal

    A modern state runs on paper. Early Meiji Japan needed it for land certificates, revenue stamps and much else. Yet the country had no Western-style paper mills or printing works. The company history speaks of Japan being plagued by floods of imported paper. A proposal to make it a government project was turned down. So Shibusawa urged a joint-stock company instead, and it was approved in February 1873.

    Meiji industry had two engines, and this walk shows both. One was private capital, organised by men like Shibusawa. The other was the state's own works, such as the army's arsenals. On a single morning you walk from the first to the second. The paper mill and the ammunition works were the two hands of the same modernising state.

    Your six questions, answered on the ground

    The walk speaks most to your first volume, on cotton and the factory. Japan here mirrors early America: a latecomer importing a revolution made elsewhere. Every one of Marx's six questions gets a concrete answer.

    Where did the starting capital come from? The company raised ¥150,000. Its backers were the Mitsui, Ono and Shimada houses, the merchant firms that handled the government's money. So the first industrial capital at Ōji was merchant money tied closely to the state. As with Moses Brown, merchant wealth moved into manufacture.

    Where did the machines come from? From Britain. The company imported British machines and hired foreign engineers at ¥200 to ¥250 a month. An American engineer led the trial run. This is technology transfer to a latecomer, the same problem Slater solved from memory in 1790.

    Who bought the product? At first, hardly anyone. The company lost over ¥40,000 by 1875. What saved it were orders from the Finance Ministry's paper-money bureau, for land certificates and revenue stamps. The state was the first customer.

    Where did the workers come from, and how were they disciplined? The company history says little about where the hands came from. It is clearer about discipline, which did not hold. In 1898 a strike by the shop-floor workers ended only when Shibusawa and his colleague Ōkawa Heizaburō resigned.

    What happened to the surplus, and to control? It went to the bank. Mitsui demanded a director in 1896 as the price of new capital. In 1903 half the share capital was written off and the same amount in new shares went to the Mitsui family. The company history says real power then passed wholly to Mitsui. The organiser was organised out.

    The arsenal answers the same questions the other way round. Its capital was the state's. It made ammunition for the army. Side by side, the two sites show state and private capital building one industrial base.

    What you will know at 12:30 that you did not know at 07:00

    You will have seen, in one ward, how a latecomer country assembled a factory system it did not invent. You will know where the money came from, whose machines turned, who bought the first output, and who ended up in charge. You will have a sharp, physical image for a chapter: a banker's garden on a hill above his mill. You will also have a test case for your first volume, seen from the far side of the world. Here the factory, the state's hunger for paper and the army's need for ammunition arrive together. The Ōji machines started in 1875, the very year Perez dates the age of steel. And you will have watched an organiser who preached public virtue lose his own company to a bank. That is "for better and worse" in a single life.

    It is a calm morning, too. Kita is a modest-income ward with few tourists. The whole day costs about ¥1,600, roughly ten dollars.

    What it asks of you

    One honest loss first. The Shibusawa Memorial Museum is shut for maintenance from 30 November 2026 to 19 February 2027. You cannot go inside the museum, the Bankōro or the Seien Bunko. Whether the old garden itself stays open during the work was not confirmed. If the gate is shut, you view the buildings from the park path. The Paper Museum and the grounds stay open.

    The walk is about six kilometres, with one hill up into Asukayama. You will be home at about 12:45, a quarter of an hour past your target. If that matters, skip the garden or eat faster. For a morning that hands you the whole circuit of capital, fifteen minutes is a fair price.

    The three morning walks: cotton, wool and the day labourers, machine shops and the towers that replaced them and paper, gunpowder and Shibusawa. The Thursday plan: five revolutions. Map tiles: 地理院タイル (GSI), 今昔マップ on the web (Tani Kenji, Saitama Univ.), 農研機構 1880s rapid survey (CC BY 2.1 JP).
